title: The Kalamas ask
hookLine: a town tired of teachers asks the Buddha whom to believe; he ends with four comforts that hold whether or not there is a next life (AN 3.65)
last: YASA'S NIGHT — WALK OUT OF THE PARTY.

lines: SENT WALKING, FOR THE GOOD OF THE MANY.
cards: Yasa's friends come, then fifty more, and soon the Buddha sends them all walking, for the good of the many. The roads of India are full of walking teachers.
In a town called Kesaputta, the people, the Kalamas, have had enough. Teacher after teacher comes through, praises his own teaching, and runs down everyone else's. Then the next one does the same.
And when the Buddha arrives, they put it to him plainly: we don't know who to believe. Even about whether there's another life at all.

teach.b: The Buddha's first answer surprises them. Your doubt is reasonable, he says. You're right to be unsure.
He goes on to give them a way to test any teaching, and we'll come back to that later on the path. Today is about the way the talk ends, the part people often skip.
He describes someone whose mind is free of hatred and ill will, clear and clean. That person, he says, has four comforts, right here in this life.

teach.h: IF THERE IS ANOTHER LIFE, IT GOES WELL.
teach.b: If there is another world, and good and bad deeds bear fruit, then I'll arise somewhere good.

teach.h: IF THERE ISN'T, THIS ONE ALREADY DOES.
teach.b: If there isn't, then here and now I live free of hostility, at ease. If harm comes to those who do harm, I intend harm to no one, so how could it touch me? And if it doesn't, I'm clean either way.
The Pali word is assasa: comfort, the kind that lets you breathe out. Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't tell the Kalamas to settle the question of rebirth before they begin.
Rebirth runs all through his teaching, and many Buddhists hold it close. But this talk starts with what anyone can see. Teachers read it in more than one way.
Some say the Buddha is meeting doubters where they are, before he teaches more.
Others take it as a welcome to begin with the question still open.
Either way, the Kalamas walk away with something they can use tomorrow morning. And if you're not sure about rebirth yet, you're in company the Buddha himself sat down with.

how: Teachers often quote the Kalama Sutta to newcomers who are unsure about rebirth; many Buddhist communities welcome people to practice while the question is still open.

o: a firm belief in the next life
comfort, a breath let out in relief
a vow of silence kept for a season

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: each praised his own, ran down the rest
this life is already at ease

s: the Buddha told the Kalamas to accept rebirth before they began
he gave them four comforts that hold whether or not there is another life.
the Buddha told the Kalamas their doubt was reasonable
the four comforts depend on a next life
the second one assumes there isn't one, and still finds ease.

games.q: you're one of the Kalamas. teacher after teacher says only he is right. one more arrives. what do you do?
o: ignore him; they're all the same.
ask him how to tell who's telling the truth.
games.why: the Kalamas asked the Buddha exactly that, and he began by telling them their doubt was reasonable.

practice: Bring to mind one big question you can't settle, about what comes after or anything else, and don't try to answer it; picture setting it down beside you, still there, still open.
Then notice what is true without the answer: the breath coming in, the breath going out, and the chance, today, to act without ill will.

wordCard.voice: Assasa. Comfort, relief, a breath let out: the four comforts the Buddha gave the Kalamas, which hold whether or not there is another life.

orig.note: Pali assasa: comfort, relief; the same word can mean breathing in, a breath of ease.

carryVoice: Your line: good either way. A life without ill will is good whether or not there's another one. Day sixty-six, done.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 3.65 (Kalama Sutta / Kesamutti Sutta): the four comforts
